messages.subject: Dividing the contribution of a certain variable
parts:
Dear INLA group,

I built a SPDE model(y ~ varA + varB + f("spde"), family="binomial") for risk mapping.
VarA is an essential variable for explaining y, but is a variable related to the individual profile and is not needed for mapping the estimated risk. VarB is a geographical factor and an important for risk mapping.
I therefore attempted to caluculate the risk excluding the contribution of varA from the model.
However, "fitted values" obtained from the inla object did not match the sum of the contributions of intercept, explanatory variables and spatial effects.
Therefore, I could not identify whether "fitted values removed the contribution of varA" or "sum of the contributions of intercept, varB and spatial effects" was appropriate for mapping.

The R-code and the plot of the relationship between the caluculated values are described below.
Why are the "fitted values" obtained from inla object and the "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters not equal?
If my understanding of the "fitted value" in inla object is incorrect, would you tell me any ideas for determining the "fitted values", excluding the contribution of varA for mapping.


Thanks!!

Amy 

↓↓↓ R code ↓↓↓

bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
                     offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
                     boundary = bd)
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))

stack <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = mydata$y),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
    data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)
  ),
  tag = "observations"
)

formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)

result <- inla(formula,
               family = "binomial",
               data = inla.stack.data(stack),
               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE, config = TRUE))

summary(result)

index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data

# "fitted values" obtained from inla object
fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]

intercept <- result$summary.fixed ["(Intercept)","mean"]
varA_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varA", "mean"] * mydata$varA
varB_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varB", "mean"] * mydata$varB

spatial_effect<-result$summary.random$spatial$mean
spatial_effect_contribution<-as.vector(A %*% spatial_effect)

# "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters
linear_predictor <- intercept + varA_contribution + varB_contribution + spatial_effect_contribution
fitted_manuals <- 1 / (1 + exp(-linear_predictor))

plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)

parts:
Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.
But due to the above fact, you wouldn’t get the same values anyway. You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn

Dear Finn,

I really appreciate your helpful comments.

I have modified the control.predictor to add "link=1" and run inla() to calculate the fitted values in consideration of the ”posterior distribution" using the R-code below.
However, the calculated fitted_values differ significantly from the values from the inla-result object.
On the other hand, the logit-transformed both values appear to be correlated.

I understand that the values will never be equal as they are derived from sampled values, but since the two values are so far apart and correlated (i.e. appear to have a constant added), I suspect that I'm missin an important element in my calculation procedure.

Could you please check the following code and plots?


Sincerely yours,


↓Rcode↓

bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
                     offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
                     boundary = bd)

  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))

stack <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = mydata$y),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)     ## !!! The variables used in the actual calculation are different from the previous one.

),
  tag = "observations"
)

formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)

result <- inla(formula,
               family = "binomial",
               data = inla.stack.data(stack),

control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))

summary(result)


index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data

# Fitted values obtained from inla object
fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]

# No. of sample
n_samples <- 1000

# sampling parameters from posterior distribution
posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, result)


fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]
 
  #Hyper parameters
  range_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Range for spatial"]
  sigma_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Stdev for spatial"]
 
  nu <- 1.5 #smooth parameter 
  d <- 2   
 
  kappa <- sqrt(8 * nu) / range_sample
 

  gamma_nu <- gamma(nu)
  gamma_nu_d2 <- gamma(nu + d / 2)
  tau_numerator <- sigma_sample * sqrt((2 * pi)^(d) * kappa^(2 * nu) * gamma_nu / gamma_nu_d2)
  tau <- 1 / tau_numerator
 
  theta1 <- log(tau)
  theta2 <- log(kappa)
 
  Q <- inla.spde.precision(spde, theta = c(theta1, theta2))
 
  # spatial random effect
  u_sample <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q))
 
  # fixed effect
  beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varA",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta2_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varB",rownames(sample$latent)))]
 
  # linear predictor(logit)
  eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * mydata$varA) + (beta2_sample * mydata$varB) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)
 
  fitted_samples[, i] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample))
}

fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)

# fitted values vs fitted manual
plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)

# calculate logit-transformed fitted values and fitted manual
logit_fitted <- log(fitted_values / (1 - fitted_values))
logit_manual <- log(fitted_manual / (1 - fitted_manual))

plot(logit_fitted, logit_manual)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Dividing the contribution of a certain variable
parts:
Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Finn

In other words:

beta1, beta2, range, sigma are a priori independent

The estimation model involves a field spatial1 with covariance parameters range, sigma, and the predictor is
  eta1=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial1
The observations are all linked to this eta1.

One can also imagine a second field spatial2 that has the same range and sigma as covariance parameters, and
  eta2=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial2

The fitted.values values output is based on 1/(1+exp(-eta1))
Your sampling procedure appears to target 1/(1+exp(-eta2))

Finn

On Mon, 28 Oct 2024 at 11:31, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Finn

Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn

Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Finn

Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.

You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn

In other words:

beta1, beta2, range, sigma are a priori independent

The estimation model involves a field spatial1 with covariance parameters range, sigma, and the predictor is

  eta2=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial2

The fitted.values values output is based on 1/(1+exp(-eta1))
Your sampling procedure appears to target 1/(1+exp(-eta2))

Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Finn

Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.
But due to the above fact, you wouldn’t get the same values anyway. You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn

Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.
But due to the above fact, you wouldn’t get the same values anyway. You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn
